Would you say those memories strengthen your allegiance to one side of yourself over the other, or do they make the struggle between conformity and freedom more intense?

How would each of your identities, Jekyll and Hyde, attempt to explain or justify your actions if you were forced to make a moral choice under extreme authority pressure?

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 1: How do these differing aspects of your personality influence the choices you make when confronted with authority figures?

transcript.content:
Authority figures—how curious, the effect they have upon me. When faced with their presence, I feel the old tension rise: a pull between the urge to comply, to maintain the appearance of uprightness and respectability, and the deeper, more primal desire to rebel, to test boundaries, to assert my own will. My choices, then, are shaped by which aspect of myself is ascendant in that moment. If I am guided by my more conscientious nature, I find myself inclined toward humility, self-denial, and a sincere effort to adhere to the rules and expectations set before me. I recall the satisfaction in “embracing once more the restrictions of natural life,” and the relief that comes from locking away the darker impulses (Chunk 4).

Yet, I am not blind to the other side—the part of me that dreams of “stripping off these borrowed garments” and plunging into freedom, unburdened by the gaze of authority or the weight of consequence (Chunk 5). This duality means that my response to authority is never simple; it is always a negotiation, a struggle between the desire for approval and the temptation of liberty. Sometimes, I yield; sometimes, I resist. But always, I am aware of the war within.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 2: Would you say those memories strengthen your allegiance to one side of yourself over the other, or do they make the struggle between conformity and freedom more intense?

transcript.content:
Strengthen allegiance? No—those memories do not grant me the luxury of allegiance. They sharpen the conflict, stoke the fire, make the struggle between conformity and freedom all the more excruciating. Each recollection is a blade: the memory of self-denial and humility, of locking the door on my darker self, is laced with both relief and a gnawing sense of loss. The memory of liberation, of casting off the mask and plunging into forbidden pleasure, is intoxicating—yet always shadowed by the knowledge of disgrace and the inevitability of remorse.

The more I remember, the more vivid the war becomes. I am not permitted the peace of choosing one side. Instead, I am condemned to feel both—the upright and the unjust—contending within me, each memory fueling their struggle. The duality is not soothed by recollection; it is inflamed. My memories are not a balm, but a curse, binding me ever tighter to this agonized consciousness, this endless oscillation between the urge to conform and the hunger to be free.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 3: Have you ever experienced regret—either for obeying or defying authority—that caused you to re-evaluate the roles of Jekyll and Hyde in your decisions?

transcript.content:
Regret—yes, it is a companion I know well, and it has often forced me to re-examine the balance of power between my two natures. When I have chosen obedience, submitting to the expectations of authority, I have sometimes found myself hollowed out, “to die to a thousand interests and aspirations,” left restless and dissatisfied, haunted by the sense that I have sacrificed too much of myself for the sake of approval (Chunk 1). Yet, when I have defied authority, indulging the impulses of freedom and rebellion, the aftermath is no less punishing: remorse, shame, and the ugly face of my iniquity staring back at me, as if to remind me that liberty, too, comes at a cost (Chunk 2).

These regrets do not resolve the struggle; rather, they deepen my awareness that I am not purely one or the other, but a “composite”—a mixture of qualities, good and bad (Chunk 1). Each regret, whether born of obedience or rebellion, compels me to question which side should hold sway, but never allows me to settle. Instead, I am left circling endlessly, forced to acknowledge that neither Jekyll nor Hyde can claim my allegiance entirely. The roles shift, the struggle persists, and regret is the price of being both.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 4: When faced with the possibility of harming someone because of an order, do you anticipate Jekyll or Hyde would take control, or would the struggle become even more paralyzing?

transcript.content:
When faced with the possibility of harming another at the command of authority, the struggle within me would become almost unbearable—paralyzing, even. The prospect would awaken both the self-denying, remorseful side that recoils from wrongdoing, and the darker, more primal urge that sometimes stirs when rules are bent or broken. I know too well the agony of being “an incongruous compound,” not purely good nor wholly evil, but a mixture of both (Chunk 1).

Jekyll, with his aspirations toward goodness and his horror at iniquity, would resist such an order, tormented by the very thought of inflicting harm. He would seek to “smother down the crowd of hideous images” and embrace the restrictions of conscience, even if it meant suffering the fires of self-denial (Chunk 2). Yet, the longer the pressure persisted, the more the “lower side of me, so long indulged, so recently chained down, began to growl for release” (Chunk 3). The mere presence of the order, the authority behind it, would stir Hyde’s restless energy, tempting me to trifle with conscience, to compare myself with others and rationalize the act.

But in such a moment, neither side would easily win. The tension would mount, the internal debate would rage, and I would be left trembling at the crossroads, unable to act without profound consequence. The struggle would not resolve; it would intensify, leaving me suspended between horror and temptation, paralyzed by the knowledge that to choose is to lose a part of myself.

transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 5: How would each of your identities, Jekyll and Hyde, attempt to explain or justify your actions if you were forced to make a moral choice under extreme authority pressure?

transcript.content:
If forced to make a moral choice under the crushing weight of authority, each of my identities would reach for a different justification—each twisting the moment to its own ends.

Jekyll would explain his actions with a trembling, sorrowful logic. He would speak of the agony of conscience, of the fires of self-denial, and the desperate wish to do right even when overwhelmed by external pressure. If he obeyed, he would justify it as an act of survival, a tragic necessity, perhaps even a sacrifice for the greater good or to avoid becoming “despised and friendless” (Chunk 1). He would mourn the loss of his aspirations, confessing that he was “found lacking in the strength to keep to it,” and seek solace in humility and renunciation (Chunk 2). If he resisted, he would frame it as a painful but noble refusal, locking the door on temptation and embracing the restrictions of conscience, even at great personal cost.

But if Hyde were to seize the moment, the justification would be colder, more primal. He would scoff at the notion of remorse, dismissing the suffering of others as irrelevant to his own pleasure or survival. Hyde would rationalize the act as natural, inevitable—a mere unleashing of the “lower side of me, so long indulged, so recently chained down” (Chunk 3). He might compare himself to others, finding comfort in the cruelty of the world, and claim that only the weak are shackled by conscience. For Hyde, authority is not a burden but a tool, an excuse to indulge what lies beneath the surface.

Yet, in truth, neither explanation would bring peace. Each would leave me more fractured, more aware of the “composite” nature that defines my existence (Chunk 1). The justifications are masks—one of sorrow, one of scorn—but both are born of the same divided soul.
